newsitem.title: USA: U.S. welcomes Israeli approval of West Bank pullback.
newsitem.headline: U.S. welcomes Israeli approval of West Bank pullback.

text.p: The United States on Thursday welcomed the Israeli Cabinet's approval of a further troop withdrawal in the West Bank, calling the decision a demonstration of Israel's commitment to the peace process.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu telephoned U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to brief her on the move.
"This decision on the first phase of further redeployment represents a serious expansion of Palestinian authority," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in a written statement.

After a seven-hour debate, the cabinet voted 10-7 to back Netanyahu's proposal to hand over another 9 percent of the West Bank to the Palestinians. Two percent of the area to be turned over comprises territory fully under Israeli control.

The withdrawal would be the first of three from mainly rural areas of the West Bank, with the last to be completed by mid-1998. Final borders are to be decided in permanent status talks scheduled to begin this month.
Burns noted that the Israeli Cabinet decision was only the first step in a three-phase process and said the United States hoped Israel would do more in the second and third phases.
"We believe this decision is a demonstration of Israel's commitment to the peace process," he said.
Israel television said Netanyahu had been under U.S. pressure to placate the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) after approving new Jewish housing in Arab East Jeruslem.
The United States on Wednesday criticised Israel for the second time in a week, calling a decision to shut down four Palestinian offices in East Jerusalem "very difficult to understand."
On Monday, President Bill Clinton chided Netanyahu for his decision to authorise a plan to build 6,500 more Jewish homes in mainly Arab East Jerusalem.
At a White House meeting with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, Clinton said he wished the decision had not been made and maintained that it would foster mistrust with the Palestinians.
Albright said in an interview earlier on Thursday the housing project had detracted from "the positive bonds" Washington wanted to create.
"We now have to move on and try to -- without making judgments -- move on to manage a relationship so they can get back on track," she said on the PBS programme "Newshour with Jim Lehrer."

Albright said the Clinton administration had made clear to Netanyahu that his approval of the housing project did not help in building the kind of positive atmosphere necessary for moving forward on the permanent status talks.
